Guaiquerí

This starting route brings together Guaiquerí historical interpretation, a named urban community case in Margarita and a maritime archive. These sources do not make every island resident part of one community.

Names & relationshipsA broader reading label related to the specifically documented El Poblado community context. It is not one government, a statement that every Margarita resident or fishing family shares an identity, or an ancestry test.
A source guide for a deeper dive.This entry provides a brief orientation and an organized reading path. A comprehensive deep dive has not yet been completed. Follow the annotated sources and distinguish primary community accounts from outside reference material.
Still unfinished

Selected actual-content works and a narrowly scoped credited Cubagua photograph provide a starting route. Fuller community-led histories and comparisons remain open; quantity does not establish completion or endorsement.

Assessment recorded October 29, 2026. This is separate from research completion and community review.

Isla Cubagua — modern island context
Rodian / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0

Source & image record ↗ · CC BY 3.0 Unported — not ShareAlike or CC0

A modern photograph identified in its source as Isla Cubagua, used as named-island geographic context for the Guaiquerí route. UCLA’s archive-project account explicitly connects Cubagua fishing communities and particularly Guaiquerí identity. This is not a portrait of a named community, a reconstruction, a historical territory, evidence that all island residents belong to one people, or an all-Margarita ancestry claim.

01

Reading the historical name

Antczak and colleagues examine how Guaiquerí labels changed under colonial rule. Their interpretation should be distinguished from an official definition of present membership.

Read the sources [1] Unidad de Estudios Arqueológicos, Universidad Simón Bolívar; Sidestone Press offprint

02

A specific community in Porlamar

Aguilera’s 2021 essay describes Guaiquerí identity in El Poblado, also called Caserío Francisco Fajardo. It treats urban cultural change as compatible with identity, rather than proof of disappearance.

Read the sources [2] Encuentro Educacional, Universidad del Zulia

03

Archives, families and maritime knowledge

The Archivo Guaiquerí project and UCLA describe preservation work on Museo Marino de Margarita collections. Inventoried materials and family memories offer future reading; an inventory is not a fully inspected public collection.

Read the sources [3] Archivo Guaiquerí / Gente de Mar; Museo Marino de Margarita project context [4] UCLA Library, Modern Endangered Archives Program

Academic / referenceUnidad de Estudios Arqueológicos, Universidad Simón Bolívar; Sidestone Press offprintSource 1

Shortened title: “Indios buenos”, “Indios malos”: identidad Indígena en el Caribe suroriental — selected chapter ↗

Publication: 2024

Read the two regional cases as a scholarly argument about changing labels, power and continuing identity, not a catalogue of timeless tribes.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual primary-hosted 48-page chapter offprint indexed body read selectively: title/author/publication pages; printed pp.139–151 / PDF pp.7–19 for approach and Caquetío/Guaiquerí colonial case discussions; selected concluding passages printed pp.155–156 and158 / PDF pp.23–24,26. Not the full chapter, bibliography, entire edited book or original colonial records.

Review recorded: October 29, 2026

Access note: Actual selected PDF body was readable in the web tool. No local original PDF or figure reuse claimed. Linguistic identity, chronology and the relation between archaeological styles and named peoples need further specialist review. No phenotype, genetic purity, sole present government or disappearance conclusion adopted.

Academic / referenceEncuentro Educacional, Universidad del ZuliaSource 2

La interculturalidad como reflexión en la dimensión heterogénea del patrimonio cultural inmaterial — selected Guaiquerí case ↗

Publication: 2021

A precise local-community example in urban Margarita, useful for distinguishing cultural change from a disappearance claim.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual normally downloaded 14-page PDF: title/abstract on PDF p.2 / printed p.143; selected case passages on PDF p.4 / printed p.145 and PDF pp.9–10 / printed pp.150–151 read. These discuss a Guaiquerí community in El Poblado/Caserío Francisco Fajardo and the author’s interpretation of cultural change. Other theoretical pages and cited underlying fieldwork were not inspected.

Review recorded: October 29, 2026

Access note: PDF is issue28(2), July–December2021; DOI/hosting record may be later, so filename2023 is not a publication-date claim. One web-tool fetch was restricted, but a single ordinary original-URL request succeededHTTP200. No ancestry purity, all-resident identity, present legal recognition, universal religion or claimed five-century date is adopted.

A substantial introduction to archive provenance and community-linked preservation; specific records remain future reading.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual project body, web lines19–75 and80–109: scope, inventory versus digitization, provenance of Cervigón/Cruxent collections, preservation process and item-specific rights warning. Catalogue contents, all individual objects, interviews and listed maps were not inspected.

Review recorded: October 29, 2026

Access note: One normal terminal request returned403 and stopped; actual body remained available through the web reader. The independent UCLA project page confirms the named project.
